claims.text: Excellent wear performance in high-entropy-alloy coatings is governed by the in situ formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or reactive-oxide nanocomposite surface layer during friction.
The wear-induced surface layer distributes frictional stresses.
The wear-induced surface layer accommodates plastic deformation through multiple deformation pathways.
Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer results in lower friction and reduced material loss.
The as-sprayed coating has a mixed microstructure containing both nanocrystalline and coarser grains.
A low-temperature annealing treatment will coarsen the coating's initial grain structure.
Coarsening the initial microstructure reduces the coating's predisposition to form a dynamic nanolayer during wear.
Mechanical shear and strain localization during sliding can drive dynamic amorphization of the near-surface material.
Limited reactive oxidation during sliding can produce a protective oxide nanocomposite or nanocrystalline glaze layer.
Wear-induced amorphization or oxidation refines the near-surface grain structure.
As-sprayed, initially fine-grained coatings will rapidly develop a protective nanolayer during wear.
As-sprayed coatings will have lower friction coefficients than pre-annealed, grain-coarsened coatings.
As-sprayed coatings will have significantly lower wear rates than pre-annealed, grain-coarsened coatings.
Dynamic nanolayer formation governs wear performance under moderate-to-high sliding loads at ambient temperature.
The proposed effect weakens when sliding speed or temperature does not permit sufficient interfacial transformation.

Comparable nanolayer formation and comparable wear performance in the as-sprayed and annealed groups would falsify the claim that initial microstructure controls wear by controlling dynamic-layer formation.
